The audit has retrieval gaps: the RFC index returned HTTP 429, as did several individual metadata and errata pages. The retrieved current entries support the planned protocol facts and the supplied replacement relationships, including TCP RFC 9293, TLS 1.3 RFC 9846, DHCPv6 RFC 9915, temporary IPv6 addresses RFC 8981, DNS terminology RFC 9499, IEEE 802 identifiers RFC 9542, service identity RFC 9525 and zone identifiers RFC 9844. This is not a claim of an exhaustive completed audit.

Additional relationships found beyond the explicitly enumerated baseline: RFC 2131 is updated by 3396, 4361, 5494 and 6842; RFC 4821 and RFC 8085 are updated by 8899; RFC 6890 is updated by 8190; RFC 2181 is updated by 2535, 4033, 4034, 4035, 4343, 5452 and 8767; RFC 2308 by 4033, 4034, 4035, 6604, 8020, 8499, 9499 and 9520; RFC 4343 by 5890; RFC 7766 by 8490 and 9103; RFC 6066 additionally by 8449 and 9325. RFC 9844 updates 4007, 7622 and 8089. RFC 8996 obsoletes 5469 and 7507; RFC 9852 updates 9325. Extra planned sources RFC 2782 and RFC 7208 are updated by 6335/8553 and 7372/8553/8616 respectively; RFC 3596 is current and unupdated. The obsolete RFC 5246 entry also lists updates 5878, 5746, 6176, 7465, 7507, 7568, 7627, 7685, 7905, 7919, 8447, 9155 and 10015; RFC 10015 was published in July 2026 and concerns TLS 1.2 key exchanges outside this plan.

Expanding the baseline's non-exhaustive lists: RFC 1034 lists updates 1101, 1183, 1348, 1876, 1982, 2065, 2181, 2308, 2535, 4033, 4034, 4035, 4343, 4592, 5936, 8020, 8482, 8767 and 9471. RFC 1035 lists 1101, 1183, 1348, 1876, 1982, 1995, 1996, 2065, 2136, 2137, 2181, 2308, 2535, 2673, 2845, 3425, 3658, 4033, 4034, 4035, 4343, 5936, 5966, 6604, 7766, 8482, 8490, 8767 and 9619. RFC 1122 lists 1349, 4379, 5884, 6093, 6298, 6633, 6864, 8029 and 9293. RFC 4271 lists 4724, 6286, 6608, 6793, 7606, 7607, 7705, 8212, 8654, 9072, 9687 and 9774. These are metadata relationships, not citations to superseded specifications for cards.

IANA dates confirmed: [IPv4 Special-Purpose Address Registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/iana-ipv4-special-registry/) 2025-10-09; [IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/iana-ipv6-special-registry/) 2025-10-09; [IPv6 Address Space](https://www.iana.org/assignments/ipv6-address-space/) 2025-10-23; [Service Names and Port Numbers](https://www.iana.org/assignments/service-names-port-numbers/) 2026-09-30; [Protocol Numbers](https://www.iana.org/assignments/protocol-numbers/) 2026-03-09; [DNS Parameters](https://www.iana.org/assignments/dns-parameters/) 2026-08-28; [ICMP Parameters](https://www.iana.org/assignments/icmp-parameters/) 2026-01-05; [ICMPv6 Parameters](https://www.iana.org/assignments/icmpv6-parameters/) 2026-06-09. The [root servers page](https://www.iana.org/domains/root/servers) describes hundreds of servers and 13 named authorities operated by 12 organizations.

Verified errata 570 and 5141 change RFC 894's erroneous minimum to maximum; the Ethernet card applies that correction and cites erratum 570. RFC 9293's verified errata are 8126, 8167, 8171 and 8710, with no change to planned facts. Other retrieved verified reports do not change the selected facts. Relevant boundaries checked include RFC 1035 errata 2130 and 6601 on TTL representation, RFC 2018 erratum 1610 on handling prior SACK information after timeout, RFC 8200 erratum 5945 on Fragment Header wording, and RFC 6890 erratum 6404 distinguishing 0.0.0.0/8 from 0.0.0.0/32; the plan avoids their affected details.

Current exhaustive errata retrieval remains incomplete for RFCs 768, 3021, 3022, 3927, 4862, 6298, 7136, 7217, 8064, 8212, 8981, 1191, 8201, 8899, 2151, 7908, 9221 and 9852. Official indexed listings were recovered for 5227, 9542, 9460 and 9499, but their live audits remain incomplete. RFC 2131's verified listing was retrieved, but individual report 7368 could not be read. RFC 1191's current maturity was not independently retrieved; RFC 8201's metadata was confirmed through an official search result. No retrieved source identifies a RFC published after 2026-10-08 that changes a planned fact; the failed index prevents an exhaustive assertion.

Successful RFC Editor page opens included info pages and/or published HTML texts for RFCs 768, 791, 792, 826, 894, 1034, 1035, 1122, 1812, 1918, 2018, 2131, 2151, 2181, 2308, 3021, 3022, 3927, 4193, 4271, 4291, 4343, 4443, 4632, 4787, 4821, 4861, 4862, 4890, 5227, 5681, 5737, 5952, 6066, 6298, 6335, 6598, 6793, 6890, 6891, 7136, 7208, 7217, 7323, 7505, 7766, 7908, 8064, 8085, 8200, 8201, 8212, 8482, 8767, 8981, 9000, 9001, 9002, 9221, 9293, 9312, 9369, 9438, 9460, 9499, 9525, 9542, 9637, 9844, 9846, 9849, 9851, 9852 and 9915, plus metadata pages for 8446, 5246 and 10015 and extra texts 3596 and 2782. Published TXT fallbacks were read for 2018, 2151, 4443, 9460, 8899, 8212, 1191 and 8201. Errata searches, individual reports and official inline-errata renderings were also opened where retrievable; inline renderings are not card references. All nine requested IANA pages were opened.

The requested MDN pages were opened: [TCP handshake](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/TCP_handshake), [QUIC](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/QUIC) and [How browsers work](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Performance/Guides/How_browsers_work). The last retains the incorrect TLS round-trip counts and the lookup shortcut to an authoritative server; neither supplies protocol evidence. One section description needs qualification: RFC 5227 permits broadcast ARP replies, so the plan avoids treating unicast replies as universal. Retrieved sources otherwise support the selected section facts.

cards.statement: The Internet protocol suite groups protocols into link, internet, transport and application layers.
cards.explanation: RFC 1122 uses these four layers to organize Internet protocols and their host requirements.

source.title: Requirements for Internet Hosts — Communication Layers

cards.statement: The Internet application layer corresponds just to the OSI application layer.
cards.explanation: The Internet application layer combines OSI application and presentation functions, plus some session functions.
cards.misconception: The Internet application layer has the same scope as OSI application.

cards.statement: IP repairs lost datagrams before passing their data to a transport protocol.
cards.explanation: IP provides a datagram service with no delivery guarantee. Higher layers supply reliability when needed.
cards.misconception: IP supplies reliable delivery.

cards.statement: In IPv4, ICMP belongs to the internet layer even though IP carries its messages.
cards.explanation: ICMP forms an integral part of IPv4; carrying ICMP inside IP does not make it a transport protocol.

cards.statement: A sender wraps a link-layer frame inside a TCP segment for transmission over Ethernet.
cards.explanation: A sender puts the TCP segment inside an IP datagram, then carries that datagram inside a link-layer frame.
cards.misconception: Link-layer frames enclose transport payloads in reverse order.

source.title: Requirements for Internet Hosts — Communication Layers

cards.statement: An Ethernet MAC address with its M bit set identifies a group of recipients.
cards.explanation: The M bit in the first octet distinguishes group destinations, including multicast and broadcast, from unicast.

source.title: IANA Considerations and IETF Protocol and Documentation Usage for IEEE 802 Parameters

cards.statement: The X bit set in an Ethernet MAC address marks an address from an IEEE-assigned global block.
cards.explanation: IEEE-assigned global MAC addresses have X equal to zero. X equal to one marks the local address space.
cards.misconception: A set X bit means universal assignment.

source.title: IANA Considerations and IETF Protocol and Documentation Usage for IEEE 802 Parameters

cards.statement: RFC 894 sets 1500 octets as the maximum IP datagram length carried over Ethernet.
cards.explanation: Verified erratum 570 corrects 'minimum' to 'maximum' in RFC 894's Ethernet data-field limit.

cards.statement: ARP's address-resolution format requires an IPv4 address as its protocol address.
cards.explanation: ARP maps addresses of an indicated network protocol to hardware addresses. Its format is generic across protocol address spaces.
cards.misconception: ARP's format is specific to IPv4.

cards.statement: An Ethernet host broadcasts an ARP request when it lacks the target's address mapping.
cards.explanation: Broadcasting the ARP request lets the station holding the target protocol address receive the query.

cards.statement: An ARP target adds the sender's mapping after it checks that the opcode is a request.
cards.explanation: In RFC 826's reception algorithm, the target learns the sender's mapping before examining the opcode.
cards.misconception: An ARP target learns the sender after recognizing a request.

cards.statement: An IPv4 host uses ARP probes to check whether a candidate address is already in use.
cards.explanation: ARP probing checks for an address conflict on the link before the host starts using the candidate IPv4 address.

cards.statement: IPv4 stores the source and destination addresses as 32-bit values.
cards.explanation: Each IPv4 address occupies four octets in the IP header.

cards.statement: In an ordinary IPv4 /24 subnet, a host uses the all-zero host part as its own unicast address.
cards.explanation: In ordinary /24 addressing, the all-zero host part identifies the subnet and is reserved rather than assigned to a host.
cards.misconception: The subnet address serves as an ordinary unicast host address.

source.title: Using 31-Bit Prefixes on IPv4 Point-to-Point Links

cards.statement: The IPv4 prefix /20 corresponds to the subnet mask 255.255.240.0.
cards.explanation: Twenty leading one bits select the prefix.

source.title: Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR): The Internet Address Assignment and Aggregation Plan

cards.statement: An IPv4 /24 leaves its first octet available for individual host addresses.
cards.explanation: A /24 fixes the first three octets; the last octet supplies the host portion.
cards.misconception: A /24 leaves its leading octet for host numbering.

source.title: Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR): The Internet Address Assignment and Aggregation Plan

cards.statement: An IPv4 /26 prefix contains 64 addresses before any host-use exclusions.
cards.explanation: Six host bits give 64 address combinations.

source.title: Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR): The Internet Address Assignment and Aggregation Plan

cards.statement: In an IPv4 /24 subnet, a destination with an all-ones host part is the subnet broadcast address.
cards.explanation: The directed broadcast address selects the subnet rather than an individual host.

source.title: Using 31-Bit Prefixes on IPv4 Point-to-Point Links

cards.statement: An IPv4 /31 point-to-point link reserves one of its addresses for directed broadcast.
cards.explanation: Both /31 addresses identify endpoints on a point-to-point link.
cards.misconception: A /31 retains a dedicated directed broadcast address.

source.title: Using 31-Bit Prefixes on IPv4 Point-to-Point Links

cards.statement: An IPv4 /32 route singles out one destination address for forwarding.
cards.explanation: A /32 fixes the entire destination address.

source.title: Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR): The Internet Address Assignment and Aggregation Plan

cards.statement: CIDR selects an IPv4 prefix length from the address's legacy class.
cards.explanation: CIDR specifies prefix lengths explicitly instead of inferring them from address classes.
cards.misconception: Address classes still determine CIDR prefix lengths.

source.title: Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR): The Internet Address Assignment and Aggregation Plan

cards.statement: An operator merges separated IPv4 prefixes into a shorter prefix that covers exactly those prefixes.
cards.explanation: A single prefix covers a contiguous block; spanning separated blocks also includes the gap.
cards.misconception: One exact aggregate covers separated blocks.

source.title: Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR): The Internet Address Assignment and Aggregation Plan

cards.statement: The IPv4 prefix 198.51.100.0/25 contains the address 198.51.100.200.
cards.explanation: 198.51.100.0/25 spans last-octet values 0 through 127.
cards.misconception: The /25 covers the complete final octet.

source.title: Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR): The Internet Address Assignment and Aggregation Plan

cards.statement: An IPv4 host uses its address and subnet mask to decide whether a destination shares its connected subnet.
cards.explanation: The host compares the masked destination with its own subnet prefix to choose direct delivery or a gateway.

source.title: Requirements for Internet Hosts — Communication Layers

cards.statement: The IPv4 address 172.31.255.1 belongs to the private-use block 172.16.0.0/12.
cards.explanation: The private-use /12 spans 172.16.0.0 through 172.31.255.255.

cards.statement: IANA classifies 100.64.0.0/10 as an RFC 1918 private-use address block.
cards.explanation: 100.64.0.0/10 is Shared Address Space, allocated separately for uses involving carrier-grade NAT.
cards.misconception: Shared Address Space belongs to RFC 1918.

source.title: IANA-Reserved IPv4 Prefix for Shared Address Space

cards.statement: The IPv4 address 127.25.0.1 belongs to the loopback block 127.0.0.0/8.
cards.explanation: Loopback covers the entire 127.0.0.0/8 block, rather than just 127.0.0.1.

cards.statement: An IPv4 router may forward 169.254.0.0/16 traffic between its external interfaces.
cards.explanation: IANA marks 169.254.0.0/16 as link-local and not forwardable between a router's external interfaces.
cards.misconception: Routers forward IPv4 link-local traffic between links.

cards.statement: In IANA's IPv4 registry, a true Forwardable value marks a block as globally reachable.
cards.explanation: Forwardable concerns routing between external interfaces; Globally Reachable concerns forwarding beyond an administrative domain.
cards.misconception: Forwardable and Globally Reachable are equivalent flags.

cards.statement: An IPv4 host sends to 255.255.255.255 when it uses the limited broadcast destination.
cards.explanation: The limited broadcast destination reaches the connected network and does not pass through routers.

cards.statement: An author may use 198.51.100.0/24 for example IPv4 addresses in documentation.
cards.explanation: RFC 5737 reserves 198.51.100.0/24 for examples to avoid conflicts with assigned operational addresses.

source.title: IPv4 Address Blocks Reserved for Documentation

cards.statement: IANA makes 240.0.0.0/4 available for ordinary IPv4 unicast address assignments.
cards.explanation: IANA lists 240.0.0.0/4 as Reserved rather than as ordinary unicast address space.
cards.misconception: The reserved upper block is ordinary unicast space.

cards.statement: RFC 1918 lets operators propagate private-network routing information across inter-enterprise links.
cards.explanation: RFC 1918 says routing information about private networks shall not propagate on inter-enterprise links.
cards.misconception: Private routing information may cross inter-enterprise links.

cards.statement: NAPT lets several private hosts share one public IPv4 address by translating transport ports.
cards.explanation: NAPT translates transport identifiers as well as addresses, distinguishing sessions that share an external address.

source.title: Traditional IP Network Address Translator (Traditional NAT)

cards.statement: A traditional NAT creates a mapping when an external host starts a session toward an unmapped private host.
cards.explanation: Traditional NAT sessions start from the private side. Inbound initiation uses a static mapping for a selected private host.
cards.misconception: Inbound initiation creates a traditional NAT mapping.

source.title: Traditional IP Network Address Translator (Traditional NAT)

cards.statement: For UDP, RFC 4787 requires a NAT to reuse an internal endpoint's existing mapping across external endpoints.
cards.explanation: RFC 4787 requires Endpoint-Independent Mapping: the same internal address and port retain their mapping across external endpoints.

source.title: Network Address Translation (NAT) Behavioral Requirements for Unicast UDP

cards.statement: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses for interfaces and sets of interfaces.
cards.explanation: The full IPv6 address contains eight 16-bit groups, even when text compression hides some groups.

cards.statement: RFC 5952 formats hexadecimal letters in IPv6 addresses as lowercase.
cards.explanation: Canonical IPv6 text uses a through f; uppercase is accepted input but differs from the standardized output form.

source.title: A Recommendation for IPv6 Address Text Representation

cards.statement: RFC 5952 allows :: to shorten a single zero group in an IPv6 address.
cards.explanation: RFC 5952 reserves :: compression for runs of at least two zero groups; a lone zero group is written as 0.
cards.misconception: Canonical :: compression applies to a lone zero group.

source.title: A Recommendation for IPv6 Address Text Representation

cards.statement: IPv6 uses broadcast addresses to reach the nodes connected to a link.
cards.explanation: IPv6 replaces broadcast addressing with multicast addressing.
cards.misconception: IPv6 retains broadcast addressing.

cards.statement: An IPv6 host uses :: as a destination to reach its own protocol stack.
cards.explanation: :: represents an unspecified address. IPv6 uses ::1 for loopback delivery to the same node.
cards.misconception: The unspecified address also serves as loopback.

cards.statement: Each IPv6 interface has at least one link-local unicast address.
cards.explanation: Link-local addresses belong to fe80::/10 and serve communication on the attached link.

cards.statement: An IPv6 zone identifier selects the link for a link-local address on a host with several links.
cards.explanation: A zone identifier distinguishes which local link contains a link-local destination when the address alone is ambiguous.

source.title: Entering IPv6 Zone Identifiers in User Interfaces

cards.statement: An IPv6 Unique Local Address has link-local scope by default.
cards.explanation: Unique Local Addresses have global scope by default. Their scope does not imply global Internet reachability.
cards.misconception: Unique Local Addresses have link-local scope.

cards.statement: IANA currently limits IPv6 unicast address assignments to the range 2000::/3.
cards.explanation: IANA reserves the remaining global unicast address space for future definition and use.
cards.volatilityNote: IANA may revise which IPv6 address-space blocks are available for unicast assignments.

cards.statement: IPv6 sends a packet for an anycast address to the whole group of assigned interfaces.
cards.explanation: An IPv6 anycast packet reaches one assigned interface, chosen as nearest by the routing protocols' distance measure.
cards.misconception: Anycast delivers one packet to the entire group.

cards.statement: An author may use 3fff::/20 for example IPv6 addresses in documentation.
cards.explanation: RFC 9637 allocates 3fff::/20 for documentation alongside the earlier documentation space.

cards.statement: RFC 7136 treats an IPv6 interface identifier as a coded description of the interface's hardware address.
cards.explanation: RFC 7136 makes interface identifiers opaque values; their bits do not generally expose underlying hardware properties.
cards.misconception: Interface identifier bits encode hardware properties.
